title: Paper manufacture, imports and acceptance around the Islamic Mediterranean
period: ca. 750–1500; later material and craft evidence used only as qualified comparators
summary: Papermaking and paper use crossed connected regions through uneven production and trade networks. Imported sheets could support writing without local manufacturing capability. Material suitability and negotiated acceptance are supported interactions; a quantified cost explanation is not established.

stages.invention: Not located here: the case concerns transmission/adaptation of an older technique, without a unique inventor or battle claim.
stages.feasibility: Broad evidence of manufacturing in Baghdad by the late eighth century and Mediterranean Christian production by the twelfth, mediated by Bloom's synthesis (NET-K01).
stages.deployment: Manufacturing history is separated from the use of Italian watermarked paper in a Tunisian royal letter of 1350 (NET-K03).
stages.diffusion: Qualitative chronology and traded-paper examples; no consistent mill, household or writing-volume denominator.
stages.scaling: Craft inputs and finishing are examined, but no cross-regional productivity or price series is available.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Religious concern about watermark imagery is documented alongside a permissive 1409 ruling, not a measured population refusal.
stages.displacement/reversal: Local manufacturing and imported paper may change relative importance; no claim that paper use ceased where domestic production contracted.

counterevidence: Bloom's diffusion and cost interpretations are partly inherited; later surviving-paper collections are not medieval production samples. A ruling does not demonstrate a subsequent rise in purchases. Cheap imports, local input scarcity and political change remain rival explanations.

episode.technology_configuration: Fibre-sheet manufacture and purchased writing paper; separate subepisodes are Islamic/Mediterranean transmission, 1350 Tunisian imported-paper use and 1409 permission. Barrett's European 1300–1800 workflow and later material samples are limited comparators.
episode.task: Produce or obtain sheets suitable for writing/printing and acceptable to the intended user.
episode.population: Historically documented producers and selected literate purchasers/users; the Tunisian court letter and juristic ruling do not sample ordinary households.
episode.interval: ca. 750–1500 for transmission/use; later manufacturing descriptions and conservation samples are not backcast as uptake measures.
contemporary_alternatives: Imported paper instead of local manufacture
Different paper grades and finishing
Parchment or papyrus for some earlier tasks, without a measured task-by-task choice set
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative production chronology and a named watermarked letter; no regional denominator. The 228-paper laboratory collection, including 133 undated samples, measures material properties rather than adoption.
episode.observation_limits: Manuscript survival, uncertain paper provenance and later craft descriptions; text language does not establish where a sheet was made.

actors.chooser: Makers select production practices; courts, scribes and purchasers choose materials within available supplies; a jurist addresses permissibility in one recorded dispute.
actors.payer: Patrons and purchasers fund texts/materials, and producers acquire equipment and inputs; cost shares and credit terms are not measured.
actors.operator_maintainer: Papermaking and finishing workers, traders and scribes; specific employment and unpaid household arrangements are not reconstructed.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers preparing materials and people reliant on patrons' documents; effects on competing material trades are not quantified.
actors.ability_to_refuse: The 1409 question indicates concern about using certain imported sheets, but actual refusals and purchasers' alternatives are unknown. No free-choice inference from eventual use.

labour.tasks: Material procurement, fibre preparation, forming, drying, sizing/finishing and writing; the evidence identifies tasks, not net job gains.
labour.entry_barriers: Craft skill, usable water/materials, equipment and trading access; relative importance and exclusion rules unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Control of workshops, water and supply routes is potentially consequential but not systematically documented in these sources.
labour.transition: No individual worker or cohort series; broad manufacturing movement cannot establish retraining duration.
labour.distribution: Evidence privileges surviving high-quality sheets and literate patrons; wages, ordinary consumers and downstream harms are not measured.
labour.evidence_limit: No occupational employment or real-income estimate, and no inference that imported supply improved every producer's livelihood.

title: Chinese woodblocks and selective movable-type use
period: 868–ca. 1850; distinct dated-object, process-testimony and later publishing subepisodes
summary: Sponsored woodblock production, an eleventh-century description of clay type and later task-specific publishing show that feasibility, use and dominance are separate. Reusable blocks and divisible craft stages could remain useful; character inventory alone does not determine every method choice.

stages.invention: The 868 Diamond Sutra is a surviving dated production, not a first-invention claim. Shen describes Bi Sheng's clay type in 1041–1048 (NET-K05–K06).
stages.feasibility: Shen's process account includes levelling, repeated common characters and alternating boards, but no independent timed trial or surviving Bi Sheng run.
stages.deployment: The Diamond Sutra's sponsor and declared distribution purpose are recorded; later scholarship identifies movable-type deployment in genealogies and imperial projects.
stages.diffusion: Woodblock predominance and movable-type niches in the comparative scholarship are qualitative; no common producer or reader denominator.
stages.scaling: Retained blocks, separated stages and reprinting can alter scheduling and inventory commitments; no universal cost coefficient is assigned.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Movable type is selectively employed, not categorically unavailable. Particular genres or court projects cannot stand for all publishing.
stages.displacement/reversal: No automatic replacement of woodblocks by type is established; coexistence is the bounded outcome.

counterevidence: Woodblocks also require cutting skill and storage; movable type has its own large-run advantages in Shen's testimony. Court subsidies and producer constraints may explain niches. Qualitative workflows do not prove that every observed choice minimised costs. A script-sensitive cost model also predicts type niches, so their existence does not disprove character-cost explanations of relative uptake (NET-S16).

episode.technology_configuration: Three separated subepisodes: Wang Jie's 868 woodblock scroll; Shen's account of Bi Sheng's clay types; later Chinese woodblock enterprises and selected movable-type genealogical/imperial projects.
episode.task: Reproduce specified texts for donation, repeat publication or institutional/private users; commercial revenue is not every sponsor's objective.
episode.population: One named religious sponsor/object, one historical technical account and selected publishing practices in comparative scholarship; no common sampled population.
episode.interval: 868; 1041–1048 as described in the late eleventh century; qualitative comparison chiefly 1450–1850.
contemporary_alternatives: Hand copying
Woodblock printing
Clay or other movable type where equipment/skills were available
Reprinting stored blocks rather than holding finished-book stock
episode.adoption_measure: Object and process testimony plus qualitative evidence of woodblock predominance and movable-type niches. Print runs, workshop counts and population readership are unavailable.
episode.observation_limits: Preservation favours some texts and patrons. Shen's reported convenience is not a measured price comparison; the later workflow survey spans heterogeneous markets.

actors.chooser: Donors, court projects and publishers choose texts and methods; workshop workers execute and adapt production.
actors.payer: The Diamond Sutra colophon names its sponsor; later patronage, court funding and commercial sales are distinct financing arrangements.
actors.operator_maintainer: Scribes, block cutters, printers, binders and type makers/compositors; maintaining reusable materials entails storage and handling.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers and prospective readers constrained by text availability, literacy, cost and patron choices; individual outcomes are not enumerated.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Evidence identifies patron/publisher choices rather than general worker or reader consent. Availability of alternative equipment and access to capital are not measured.

labour.tasks: Copy preparation, carving, sorting/composition, printing, binding and storing blocks/types. Methods reorganise tasks rather than eliminating skilled work altogether.
labour.entry_barriers: Literacy/calligraphy, cutting or type skills, working materials, premises and access to patrons/distribution; no wage or training-duration panel.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Control may lie with sponsors, officials or publishers; separable stages allow different work arrangements but do not establish bargaining gains.
labour.transition: No tracked artisans moving between manuscript, block and type work; long coexistence does not measure an individual transition time.
labour.distribution: A donated religious text and a commercially sold book have different beneficiaries and success measures; access and earnings by class/gender remain underobserved.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer national employment, universal cheapness, optimality or literacy from surviving editions or qualitative predominance.

title: Korean metal printing, manuscripts and rental circulation
period: 1377–early nineteenth century; Jikji and later Chosŏn subepisodes kept distinct
summary: The 1377 metal-type Jikji and 1378 woodblock version establish adjacent production methods. Later Chosŏn manuscripts served rental, imported-text access and selective literary circulation. State resources could sometimes support private publishing, so neither invention nor a state/market binary predicts a single trajectory.

stages.invention: No first-ever metal-type claim: BnF describes the surviving second volume of the 1377 Jikji.
stages.feasibility: The Jikji artifact attests actual metal-type production at Heungdeok-sa; a 1378 woodblock counterpart is a separate production.
stages.deployment: Later examples include elite female/palace novel circulation, rental manuscripts, literary collections and private use of official publishing resources (NET-K10–K12).
stages.diffusion: Commercial rental manuscript circulation from the mid-eighteenth century is documented qualitatively, without an all-reader denominator.
stages.scaling: Rental businesses and copying can circulate texts without identical mechanical editions; output volume and affordability are not measured.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Print and copying serve overlapping but different audiences and purposes; selected/variant manuscripts are not merely failed printing attempts.
stages.displacement/reversal: A general replacement of manuscripts by print is not established by the inspected evidence.

counterevidence: Expense or shortage of printed books can still explain particular copying. State support coexists with restrictions; a few private uses of official resources do not measure net openness. Prestigious surviving editions are not a representative readership sample.

episode.technology_configuration: Temple metal-type and woodblock Jikji editions (1377/1378), followed separately by Chosŏn manuscript rental/literary production and selected state/private resource transfers.
episode.task: Transmit Buddhist texts, vernacular fiction, imported Chinese works or tailored literary collections; these are distinct tasks with different users.
episode.population: One surviving edition tradition; later elite/palace women, literati, rental readers and publishing actors represented in Park's source cases, not all Koreans.
episode.interval: 1377–1378 artifacts; late seventeenth-century elite vernacular manuscript circulation; mid-eighteenth-century rental expansion and later literary practices.
contemporary_alternatives: Metal-type printing
Woodblock editions
Hand copying and selective compilation
Renting or borrowing rather than owning books
Acquiring imported printed texts where available
episode.adoption_measure: Surviving objects and qualitative descriptions of circulation practices. No common print-run, ownership, rental or literacy denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Later manuscript practices cannot measure fourteenth-century diffusion. Genre/language and class differ; copying survival and official catalogues select what can be observed.

actors.chooser: Temple patrons, court/official producers, literati, family readers and rental businesses make different text/form decisions.
actors.payer: Patrons, public resources, households, publishers and rental customers; specific fees, subsidies and cost shares are not compiled.
actors.operator_maintainer: Type makers/printers, block cutters, scribes and rental custodians; copying may involve paid or unpaid work, not consistently distinguished in inspected passages.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Potential readers excluded by cost, language or education and labourers whose work is controlled by patrons; group-level effects unknown.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Reader/publisher alternatives vary by access and social position. The existence of rental or private production does not establish universal choice or free entry.

labour.tasks: Casting/composing, carving, copying, selecting and changing texts, editorial work and lending. Manuscript publication sustains work distinct from serial reproduction.
labour.entry_barriers: Literacy, access to texts and official equipment, craft expertise, social networks and capital; no comparable entry-cost data.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Some actors reuse state expertise/type privately, but who could obtain such access and on what terms is only partly documented.
labour.transition: No artisan cohort or earnings record ties the Jikji episode to later rental businesses; the long interval is explicitly not a continuous labour transition.
labour.distribution: Park identifies differentiated literary and vernacular settings, including some women readers, without implying equal female access or population-wide gains.
labour.evidence_limit: No net occupational displacement or wage claim; manuscript persistence is not direct evidence of preference, efficient choice or commercial freedom.

title: European city printing enterprises and local competition
period: 1450–1600; later city outcomes are used only within the cited study designs
summary: European presses required mobile expertise, finance and customers. City adoption and edition datasets support more discriminating analysis than an invention chronology, but their units are not readers and their causal designs require substantive assumptions. Local production and distribution conditions remain consequential after technical feasibility.

stages.invention: The analysis starts from the mid-fifteenth-century press cluster; uncertainty about early casting details is retained, rather than assigning a complete modern system to one moment.
stages.feasibility: Operating presses establish local technical capability, not financially sustainable shops everywhere.
stages.deployment: Dittmar compiles 205 adopting cities in 1450–1500; these are installations/locations, not household adopters (NET-K13).
stages.diffusion: Table I compares these with 1,811 historical cities selected by an ever-5,000-resident criterion across 1000–1800, not a contemporary census.
stages.scaling: Edition and price analyses examine local entry/competition and output in printing cities; editions differ from copies sold.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Forty of the hundred largest cities lacked presses in 1500 according to the cited historical discussion; city size is not sufficient.
stages.displacement/reversal: The contribution does not infer complete manuscript displacement or that every workshop survived.

counterevidence: Printer location is selected by demand and other institutions. Mainz distance and printer deaths may influence outcomes through channels other than print adoption/competition. City population growth may include redistribution rather than aggregate welfare gains.

episode.technology_configuration: European urban press enterprises with operators, materials, finance and book distribution; two studies use different units and samples.
episode.task: Produce and sell texts; study outcomes include adoption location, edition output, purchasing prices and city/institutional change rather than a single success measure.
episode.population: Historical European cities in the specified catalogues; price observations from selected purchases and printer biographies are separate subpopulations.
episode.interval: Adoption 1450–1500; competition/output mainly the sixteenth century; outcome windows follow each cited design and are not pooled.
contemporary_alternatives: Imported printed books
Manuscript copying
Nearby-city production and distribution
No local press despite continued book use
episode.adoption_measure: 205 adopting cities; Table I comparison base of 1,811 historical cities. Separate edition, purchaser-price and biography data; regression samples differ. No reader denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Catalogue survival, historical-city selection, incomplete biographies and a selected price collection. The 2019 introduction and §3.1 report different edition totals, not silently harmonised.

actors.chooser: Printers/investors choose entry, locations and output; purchasers and institutional clients choose among available books.
actors.payer: Workshop investors/creditors and purchasers; working capital precedes sale. Sources describe financial constraints without a complete capital-cost series.
actors.operator_maintainer: Trained printers, compositors and related craftspeople; paper and distribution workers also contribute, with exact staffing varying by shop.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers, competing producers and people affected by disseminated content; city-level effects do not identify who benefited or was harmed.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Firm entry and consumer purchases occur under uneven resources, literacy and local regulation; no blanket claim of free entry, unrestricted print or informed consent.

labour.tasks: Type preparation/composition, press operation, correction, financing and selling; movement of trained printers spreads skill. No net employment effect is estimated here.
labour.entry_barriers: Apprenticeship/tacit expertise, capital and reliable customers; machinery availability alone does not establish feasible entry.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Shop ownership and competition influence prices and output; wage bargaining and workers' shares of gains are not identified by the city models.
labour.transition: Printer biographies support mobility/entry analysis, but no complete worker retraining or displaced-scribe cohort is followed.
labour.distribution: Local price/output effects need not equal benefits for all groups; literacy, subject access and migration complicate distributional inference.
labour.evidence_limit: Population growth and publication counts cannot supply wages, national productivity, welfare or universal occupational predictions.

title: Ottoman printed-book permissions and Müteferrika's market
summary: An alleged blanket printing ban is not established by the inspected documentary critique. Actual permissions were actor- and subject-specific. Müteferrika's reconstructed output, estate stock and selected probate ownership show production/circulation, but do not measure exact sales or mass readership.

stages.invention: No invention claim; multiple Ottoman printing communities and imported books predate the particular press studied.
stages.feasibility: Existing printed books and Müteferrika editions demonstrate production; legal permission and market viability remain distinct.
stages.deployment: The 1588 firman protects specified imported-book trade; the 1727 grant authorises a particular enterprise with subject/correction conditions.
stages.diffusion: Sixteen of 335 selected Istanbul askeri probate inventories with more than three books contain the studied prints, 1724–1748; not a population adoption rate.
stages.scaling: Sabev reports 8,200 initial copies for thirteen known-run editions and estimates three other runs; 2,981 copies remain in the estate. Production minus stock is not observed sales.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Title choices, subject limits, price and distribution constrain the observed market; motives and effects are not isolated.
stages.displacement/reversal: Neither universal commercial failure nor replacement of manuscripts is demonstrated; residual stock and circulation coexist.

counterevidence: Missing blanket-ban documents do not establish an absence of narrower restrictions. Some owners were religious officials. Initial runs are partly estimated, gifts remove stock without sales, and probate inventories privilege particular deceased owners.

episode.technology_configuration: Three distinct evidential units: a 1588 protection for merchants' printed Arabic books; the 1727 permission/fatwa; Müteferrika's output/estate and selected Istanbul ownership records.
episode.task: Authorise, reproduce, market and acquire particular texts with acceptable textual accuracy; not all Ottoman printing or religious literature.
episode.population: Named protected merchants, the permitted press and 335 selected askeri decedents with more than three books in the studied Istanbul registers.
episode.interval: 1588 permission; press activity examined mainly 1726–1746; ownership sample 1724–1748, with unequal title exposure times.
contemporary_alternatives: Manuscript books
Imported printed books
Other Ottoman printing communities and title markets, not counted as failed exposure
Borrowing or gifts rather than purchase
episode.adoption_measure: Known-run output of 8,200 copies across thirteen editions, three estimated additional runs, 2,981 estate copies; sixteen positive selected probates among 335. None is a complete sales/reader rate.
episode.observation_limits: Original register not independently recounted; gifts, valuation/finishing differences, title ages, archive selection and living/non-owning readers prevent simple sell-through or literacy estimates.

actors.chooser: The press's petitioners/publishers choose titles subject to the grant; authorities delimit permission; buyers/recipients choose or receive available works.
actors.payer: Enterprise resources and purchasers, with gifts removing stock without sales; original funding and profit accounts are incomplete.
actors.operator_maintainer: Printing workers and appointed learned correctors; source passages establish correction requirements more clearly than everyday staffing or remuneration.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Scribes, excluded authors/readers and workers may be affected; no numerical livelihood or suppression effect is established.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Formal subject and correction conditions bind this project. Individual purchasers' alternatives and coercion are not inferred from ownership; absence of a blanket ban is not universal freedom.

labour.tasks: Text selection, printing, learned correction, finishing and distribution; manuscript copying remains an alternative.
labour.entry_barriers: Authorisation for this enterprise, resources, linguistic/craft competence and customers. The evidence does not establish uniform empire-wide entry rules.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Press ownership and official validation shape control, but workers' bargaining power and occupational earnings are not documented here.
labour.transition: Estate and selected ownership snapshots do not track scribes becoming printers or individual livelihood transitions.
labour.distribution: The sample includes some religious functionaries but excludes most ordinary/non-owning readers; no social-class or gender incidence estimate.
labour.evidence_limit: No exact profit, national literacy effect, wholesale scribal displacement or quantified welfare comparison between manuscripts and print.

title: Indian Ocean navigation as instruments, route knowledge and pilot access
period: ca. 1400–1560, with a separately bounded Malindi departure in April 1498
summary: Arabic/Turkish textual navigation combines route-specific seasonal knowledge, stellar methods and instruments, with uncertain carriage prevalence. A 1498 voyage narrative shows the use of a local pilot alongside coercion in obtaining assistance. Operating knowledge and access to people cannot be reduced to possession of one device.

stages.invention: Surviving manuals and later descriptions are not invention dates for compass, altitude instruments, routes or oral knowledge.
stages.feasibility: Prescribed methods and the narrated crossing demonstrate particular operational practices, not a measured instrument accuracy or safety rate.
stages.deployment: Texts discuss stellar directions and measurement aids; the 1498 account records departure from Malindi with a supplied pilot.
stages.diffusion: No fleet-level instrument-carriage denominator. Sources differ on magnetic compass prevalence and share much of their underlying corpus.
stages.scaling: Knowledge transmission through texts, verse and pilots is examined qualitatively; no training-capacity or trade-volume attribution.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Absence of maps attached to one corpus does not prove universal chartlessness. A compass is not made a universal ocean-voyage prerequisite.
stages.displacement/reversal: Imported or standardising instruments coexist with stellar conventions and regional expertise; replacement of pilot knowledge is not established.

mechanisms: diplomacy and coercion in skill access
counterevidence: Prescription does not prove practice on every vessel. Instruments' relative accuracy and actual carriage remain unmeasured; charts may not survive. The single pilot episode cannot isolate the causal contribution of coercion or a pilot to success.

episode.technology_configuration: Late medieval/early modern northern Indian Ocean routes using seasonal/stellar knowledge with optional measurement aids; separate 1498 Portuguese fleet episode acquires a Malindi-provided pilot.
episode.task: Choose departure windows, bearings and routes and manage local hazards; the fleet episode concerns one departure/crossing rather than all ocean exploration.
episode.population: Pilots and practices represented in Ibn Majid/al-Mahri/Sidi Ali Reis textual traditions and one anonymous voyage narrative. Many East African and Asian crews are underrepresented.
episode.interval: Main textual comparison ca. 1400–1560; Malindi events 22–24 April 1498 are separately scoped.
contemporary_alternatives: Stellar directions and observations without a magnetic instrument
Fingers or wooden altitude aids
Text, verse, oral instruction or charts where available
Recruiting local pilots rather than treating all expertise as portable equipment
episode.adoption_measure: Documented prescriptions and one narrated use of a pilot. No compass-carriage, chart-use, crew-training, voyage-failure or all-ship denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Unequal textual survival, shared source traditions, translation choices and normative instructions; the chronicler's religious identifications are unreliable.

actors.chooser: Captains, ship patrons and pilots choose routes and assistance within weather, political and skill constraints; the Malindi ruler supplies a pilot in the narrated episode.
actors.payer: Voyage patrons and trading interests provide resources, but the pilot's remuneration and general training/maintenance costs are not established in the inspected passages.
actors.operator_maintainer: Pilots, navigators and crews interpret observations and maintain vessel/instruments; knowledge cannot be assigned solely to the captain.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Crews, passengers and coastal actors bear risks; the seized Malindi court servant is directly subjected to coercion in the reported episode.
actors.ability_to_refuse: The seizure constrains the servant and applies pressure to the court. The pilot's own consent/remuneration is unknown, and no universal account of coercive recruitment follows.

labour.tasks: Observe stars/winds, measure, recall or consult route instructions, recruit pilots and apply local knowledge; instrument possession does not remove interpretive work.
labour.entry_barriers: Experience, route knowledge, learning networks and access to ships/instruments; formal credential, training duration and class/gender exclusions are not systematically measured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Local knowledge can make pilots valuable, but coercion and political mediation complicate bargaining. One episode does not quantify their power or earnings.
labour.transition: No longitudinal evidence follows crews adapting to new instruments or old pilots losing work; coexistence cannot establish transition speed.
labour.distribution: Commercial interests, crews and coerced coastal actors face different returns and risks; voyage completion alone cannot aggregate these into welfare.
labour.evidence_limit: No comparative safety/accuracy effect, employment forecast, standard wage or general claim that pilot recruitment required violence.
